title: Differential Fine-Tuning for Diverse Reasoning
one_liner: Instead of tuning all weights the same way for all reasoning tasks, tune each weight differently depending on whether it helps one task or both.
lead: When you teach a language model to solve multiple types of reasoning problems at once (like math, logic, and code), the training pulls on the same weights in contradictory directions. This paper discovers that each reasoning skill uses some unique weights and shares others, and by updating them with different strengths, the model keeps all skills sharp instead of trading one off against another.

paras: A single large language model needs to answer many kinds of questions: math problems, logic puzzles, code generation. You can teach it all three by collecting datasets for each and mixing them together, then training on the mix. But the weights (the numerical knobs inside the model) get pulled in opposite directions. Training hard on math might weaken code ability, and training on logic might weaken both. The model is stuck: it has to choose which skills to sacrifice.

A beginner might try training on each dataset separately and averaging the results, or training on one task then another in order. Both fail: averaged models are neither fish nor fowl, and sequential training (learn task A, then task B) causes the model to forget task A by the time task B is finished. The problem is that all weights are being changed uniformly, so a weight that benefits math but hurts logic gets tugged equally hard in both directions, creating a standoff.

callout.html: Training a model on multiple reasoning tasks pulls weights in conflicting directions, degrading performance on every task.

steps.text: Train on one task alone, watch which weights shift, rank them by importance to that skill.
Do the same for every other reasoning task, build a map of exclusive vs shared weights.
For each weight, decide its update strength based on exclusivity: strong if only one task needs it (changing it will not break others), mild if shared (changing it risks breaking neighbors).
Feed all reasoning datasets at once, but tug each weight with its assigned strength.
Model learns all skills without forgetting, beating single-task training on each skill.

paras: The paper changes how hard each weight gets tuned when learning from mixed datasets. Instead of moving every weight equally, it moves a weight more aggressively if that weight matters only to one reasoning task (because pushing it hard will not injure other tasks), and more gently if the weight helps multiple tasks (because pushing it hard risks breaking one of the other skills that depend on it).

hidden.h2: How much each weight is needed only by one skill
hidden.name: exclusive vs shared weight importance
paras: This paper measures a quantity most prior work never names: for each weight, how much does that weight matter to this specific reasoning task compared to all the other tasks? Some weights are hired specialists (only math cares about them), while others are generalists (both math and logic benefit). The paper calls this the exclusive importance — how much this weight is uniquely valuable to this one task.

The paper estimates it by training on one task alone, measuring the gradient (which way the weight needs to move to improve on that task) and the importance based on how much the loss would worsen if you slightly moved that weight. A high exclusive importance means: change this weight boldly for this task, it will not hurt others. A low exclusive importance means: be careful, other tasks depend on this too.

heat.caption: Darker weights are more exclusively important to one task. Light weights are shared and risky to move.

reads.html: Each reasoning task needs some weights that only it uses (move those fearlessly) and some weights shared with other tasks (move those carefully so you do not break the neighbors).

The paper measures how important each weight is to each single task (by looking at how much the error would grow if you nudged the weight), then uses this exclusive importance score to adjust how aggressively each weight is tuned during multi-task training.

paras: The reason this works comes down to interference. When a weight is shared (both math and logic depend on it), tuning it for math alone might accidentally break logic. But when a weight belongs only to math, tuning it hard for math creates no collision. So the algorithm learns to ask: for each weight, in this batch of mixed tasks, how much does only this current task need this weight? If only math needs it, push it hard. If logic also needs it, push gently so logic does not get hurt.

By measuring exclusive importance beforehand (before mixed training starts), the algorithm knows which weights are safe to move boldly and which are pinch-points. Shared weights become gatekeepers — they are tuned conservatively, preserving all the skills that use them. Exclusive weights become specialists — they are tuned fully, becoming efficient tools for their one skill. The result is that all tasks improve at once, because no weight is being ripped in opposite directions.

stages.s: Identify which task owns each weight
Tune shared weights gently, exclusive weights boldly
All reasoning skills improve, because no weight is torn in opposite directions

math.words: For each weight in task T, the penalty for moving it is scaled by how much it matters only to task T, not to other tasks.
symbols: one of the reasoning tasks (math, logic, code)
how much weight i matters only to task T (1=very, 0=shared)
the current value of weight i
the value of weight i before this task was trained

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Weight w1 (math-only): exclusive_importance = 3.0, moved from 50 to 52 (change = 2) -> penalty = 3.0 * 2^2 = 12.0
Weight w2 (shared): exclusive_importance = 0.5, moved from 50 to 52 (same change = 2) -> penalty = 0.5 * 2^2 = 2.0
Same movement, but w1 is punished 6x harder, so training leaves w1 free to move for its task.

math.note: Higher exclusivity means the weight is allowed to move boldly for its task; lower exclusivity means the penalty is strong, forcing the update to stay small and preserve other tasks.

items.html: If the exclusive importance scores are computed incorrectly (e.g., from too little data or on the wrong kind of examples), the algorithm tunes the wrong weights boldly. If a math-only weight is actually shared, tuning it hard will break logic and the user will not know why.

If one reasoning task is much larger (more examples) than the others, it will still pull weights more often during training, even with differential scaling. The rarer tasks may still regress because they are updated less frequently.
The exclusive importance is measured before mixed training. If you add a fourth reasoning task that uses many of the math-only weights, they are no longer truly exclusive and will conflict again.

Use a held-out validation set of each reasoning task to measure exclusive importance (not the training data), and recompute importance when the task mix changes. Keep validation loss for all tasks monitored during training to catch interference early.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy model on three small reasoning tasks: (1) simple arithmetic (add two numbers), (2) logic puzzles (if A then B, what is C?), (3) substring matching. Train it three ways: separately on each task, all mixed with standard training, and all mixed with differential fine-tuning. For each approach, measure accuracy on a held-out test set for each task after training.
demo.metric_eq: task_retention_score = (math_acc_after + logic_acc_after + code_acc_after) / 3, no skill falls below its single-task baseline
demo.closing: The metric to watch is whether all three skills improve together without any task regressing below its single-task performance, because exclusive weight tuning prevents one task from cannibalizing another. Standard mixed training will show one or two skills drop sharply; differential tuning will hold all three flat or rising.
